opus-5.5.text:
I think they're two sides of the same coin, and that's what makes this moment so exciting.

The biggest bottleneck in robot learning has always been data. In vision and language we had the internet, billions of images and documents. In robotics there's no equivalent. Teleoperation is the standard way to collect demonstrations, but it's slow and expensive. You need a robot, an operator, and a lab, and you scale roughly linearly with the hours people put in. That won't get us to the scale we've seen in other fields.

Meanwhile, the largest source of physical interaction data in the world is people just living their lives: cooking, folding laundry, assembling things, all of it. With wearables, egocentric cameras, and smart glasses, we can capture that passively and cheaply. The question has always been how a robot learns from it when its body is so different from ours. That's the embodiment gap.

This is where humanoids come in. The closer the robot's form is to the human body, with two arms, a head-mounted camera at roughly eye level, hands that move in human-like ways, the smaller that gap gets. Human video stops being "someone else's experience" and becomes something close to the robot's own experience from a slightly different body. A human reaching into a cabinet can map fairly directly onto a humanoid doing the same thing. So the humanoid form makes human data much more useful.

It goes the other way too. A humanoid without a big data source is just expensive hardware. The real argument for building robots in our image, beyond "the world is designed for humans," is that it lets us tap into this enormous reservoir of human behavior. Human data is what makes the humanoid bet pay off.

In our own work we've treated human data as a first-class source, not just a pretraining afterthought. We co-train policies on human and robot data, align the observation and action spaces, use egocentric views for both, and represent actions in ways that transfer, like hand and end-effector trajectories in a shared frame. What we consistently see is that a little robot data plus a lot of human data beats robot data alone, especially for generalizing to new scenes and objects. The robot data grounds the dynamics and the human data supplies breadth.

I don't think we should pretend the gap is gone. Human hands are still far more dexterous than most robot hands, we have touch, and we're much more compliant. There are also real questions about how much of what a person does is intent versus incidental motion. But the direction is clear: as hardware gets more human-like and capture gets more scalable, the two reinforce each other. Better embodiment makes human data more transferable, and more human data makes the embodiment worth building.

So my view is that it's not humanoids or human data. Together they're probably our most promising path to robots that work in the messy, open-ended human world.

r001.rationale: The response says human data is what makes the humanoid bet pay off and argues that humanoid embodiment gives robots access to a vast reservoir of human behavior.

r002.rationale: The response explains that human data is harder to transfer when a robot’s body differs from a human’s, and that a more human-like humanoid form narrows this embodiment gap.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that these two things are kind of a package deal, and you can't really have one without the other.

Start from the data side. Robotics has always had a data problem. We don't have an internet of robot actions the way vision and language had an internet of images and text. So where does the data come from? The most abundant source of embodied behavior on the planet is people. Billions of hours of humans manipulating objects, moving through cluttered spaces, using tools. If we could tap into that, even a fraction of it, it would dwarf anything we could collect with robots teleoperated in a lab.

But there's a catch. Human data is only useful to a robot if the robot can actually relate to it. If I show a six-axis arm with a parallel-jaw gripper a video of a person folding a shirt with two hands and ten fingers, there's an enormous gap. The robot has to solve a correspondence problem, retargeting, before it can learn anything. Historically a lot of research effort has gone into bridging that gap, and it's hard.

That's where humanoid embodiment comes in. If the robot's body is roughly shaped like ours, that gap shrinks dramatically. The kinematics are similar, the reachable workspace is similar, the way you'd approach a drawer or a countertop is similar. Suddenly human video, motion capture, even someone wearing a glove or a headset becomes a much more direct supervisory signal. The embodiment is what unlocks the data.

And it goes the other way too. The reason humanoids are worth building, beyond the aesthetics, is precisely that they can learn from us. A humanoid without human data is just a very expensive and very hard-to-control robot. The form factor only pays off if you have a scalable way to teach it, and that scalable way is human data. So the embodiment justifies the data, and the data justifies the embodiment.

I'd add one nuance, because I think people sometimes oversimplify this. Human data gives you the "what" very well. What to do, roughly how to move, what the sequence of a task looks like. It's much weaker on the "how" at the level of contact and force. A video of someone opening a jar doesn't tell you how hard they're gripping. So I don't think human data replaces robot data. I think of it as pretraining. You use human data to learn priors, intent, and structure, and then you use a comparatively small amount of real robot interaction to close the loop on the physics the video can't show you.

The exciting part for me is that for the first time these pieces are lining up. The hardware is getting good enough, the learning methods can absorb heterogeneous data, and the human data is essentially free. We're going to see what happens when you connect all three.

r001.rationale: The response says humanoids are worth building because they can learn from people, and that human data is what makes the form factor pay off.

r002.rationale: It explains that a conventional arm faces a large correspondence and retargeting gap when learning from human actions, while humanoid embodiment shrinks that gap.

astra-6.text:
I think they enable each other in a pretty natural way. We build humanoid robots partly because our world is designed for humans—the tools, the spaces, the tasks. But having a body that’s similar to ours also makes human behavior a more useful source of data. When a person demonstrates something, the robot has a more direct correspondence between what it observes and what it might do.

That doesn’t mean you can watch a human video and simply copy the motion. The robot has different physical capabilities, and video doesn’t tell you everything about contact, force, or how an action feels. So human data can provide a starting point—what the task is, what steps might work—but the robot still needs experience interacting with the world to ground that knowledge in its own body.

The exciting part is that feedback loop: human data helps robots acquire useful behaviors, and robot experience helps us understand which parts of human behavior transfer and where additional learning is needed. Humanoid embodiment makes that connection closer, although it isn’t necessarily the best choice for every task.

r001.rationale: The response says human-designed tools, spaces, and tasks motivate humanoid robots, and that similar bodies make human behavior more useful data. It does not argue that access to human data gives humanoid embodiment its purpose.

r002.rationale: It explains that a similar body creates a more direct correspondence between human demonstrations and robot actions, conveying that human-data transfer is harder without humanoid embodiment.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they reinforce each other. A humanoid has a body that’s similar to ours, so human behavior becomes a useful source of information: how we move, how we manipulate objects, how we interact with the environment. And if we can learn effectively from that data, it makes the humanoid form more useful, because we don’t have to collect every skill from scratch on a robot.

But having a similar body doesn’t mean you can directly copy human motion. The robot has different dynamics, different sensing, different limitations. If I watch someone pick up a cup, I can see the motion, but I can’t necessarily see the forces or all the little corrections they’re making. So there’s still a gap between observing a human doing something and having a robot reliably do it.

The opportunity is to use human data to learn useful priors—what to do, what interactions matter—and then use robot experience to ground those priors in what the hardware can actually execute. As that transfer gets better, humanoid embodiment lets us take greater advantage of human data, and human data helps us build more capable humanoids.

r001.rationale: The response says a humanoid’s human-like body makes human behavior useful data and that learning from this data makes the humanoid form more useful.

r002.rationale: It describes a gap between observing human behavior and executing it on a robot, but does not state that transfer is harder without humanoid embodiment.
